text: The blade stays where the hand holds it, while the shavings curl away and fall. Kenaz is the steady edge that takes wood off until a shape stands clear. What you cut away is not lost, it is simply no longer part of the thing. Something in your work may already have its form, Kuky, waiting on your eye to admit it.

The blade stays where the hand holds it, and the shavings curl away one after another. Kenaz is the light that comes from cutting back, not from adding. What falls away, Kuky, was never the thing you were making. You may already see the shape under the wood more clearly than you did, and that is harder to unsee than to find.

The blade stays where the hand holds it, while the shavings curl away and fall. Kenaz is the cutting that takes away wood until the shape stands clear. What drops to the floor was part of the thing you are making, and it is not waste. Something you are shaping may already be clearer than you have admitted, and that clarity asks something of you.

The blade stays where the hand holds it, and everything else curls away in pale shavings. Kenaz is the cut that takes away, so the shape beneath can be seen. What falls to the floor was part of the work too, and it is not the work. Perhaps something you are making is already clearer than you have admitted, and the seeing is now yours to answer.

Your needles keep moving, though the yarn shortens with every row. Nauthiz is what works with the little that is left, and counts it. The pattern you had in mind, Kuky, meets the length you actually hold. What you are making may need one thing you cannot spin from what you have.

The needles keep moving, though the ball of yarn has shrunk to a few turns. Nauthiz is the work that goes on while the supply runs thin, and counts every stitch. You are near the end of something, Kuky, and the counting has begun. What you are making may need more than you have, and saying so is not failure.

The needles keep moving, though the yarn coiled at your feet has thinned to a last few turns. Nauthiz is the work continuing while the supply runs low, and the counting that begins. You are not measuring rows now, you are measuring what is left. What you are making may need something you do not have, and saying so is not the end of it.

The needles keep moving, though the ball of yarn has gone thin in your hand. Nauthiz is the work that continues while the supply runs short, and the shape it forces on the making. You are counting stitches now, Kuky, not by choice but because the length decides. What you are making may be asking for more than you have, and that shortage may be the only honest measure of what it needs.

The sweater lies finished on the table, the needles set aside, the basket of wool empty. Jera is the slow turn from wound yarn to worn wool, one row at a time. Nothing in it was quick, and nothing in it was wasted. Something you began before you knew its shape may now be finished, Kuky, and it is yours to judge whether it fits.

The finished sweater on the table, the needles, the spent yarn — then only the sweater. Every stitch was made on a separate evening, and none of them looked like this. Jera is the slow turn from work into something worn. What you are making now may already hold the hours you gave it before you knew its shape.

The sweater lies finished on the table, wool and lamplight and long evenings all behind it, and then only the sweater remains. Jera is the slow turning of work into something that holds its own shape. Every row was made months before you could see the whole of it. What you are shaping now may already be further along than it looks from where you sit.

The sweater is finished, and the whole winter is in it — the counted rows, the dropped stitch, the wool that smelled of sheep. Then all of it falls away but the weight of it across your hands. Jera is the season closing its own circle, work becoming a thing you can wear. What you are making now may already be holding a warmth you began long before you could name it.
